1H (Number Theory)

Words: 165 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 165
1H OurBigBook.com
Write n=2rm with m odd. If m>1, the polynomial factor of Xm+1 by X+1, evaluated at X=102r, supplies a proper divisor. Therefore n must be a power of two. Conversely this is only a necessary condition for primality testing.
For a prime factor p of the number, p is odd and does not divide 10. Its multiplicative order d satisfies d∣2n but d∤n, since 10n≡−1(modp). When n is a power of two, every proper divisor of 2n divides n, so d=2n. By Lagrange theorem in the multiplicative group of a finite field, 2n∣p−1. Thus p≡1(mod2n)​.
The Fermat factorization method searches for a difference of two squares: starting at a=⌈N​⌉, increase a until a2−N=b2, and return (a−b)(a+b). Every factorization of an odd integer has this form, with a=(d+e)/2 and b=(e−d)/2. For N=10001, the successive differences at a=101,102,103,104,105 are 200,403,608,815,1024. The last is 322, giving 10001=73⋅137​. Trial division by the primes up to their respective square roots confirms that both factors are prime.

Words: 182
2I OurBigBook.com
For nonempty compact sets, define the distance from a point to a closed set by d(x,B)=minb∈B​∣x−b∣ and the Hausdorff distance by
dH​(A,B)=max{supa∈A​d(a,B),supb∈B​d(b,A)}.
(1)
The minima and suprema exist: the sets are nonempty and compact, and the distance function is Lipschitz continuous. The Hausdorff distance is finite, nonnegative and symmetric. If it is zero, every point of A belongs to the closed set B and conversely, so A=B; the converse is immediate.
For a∈A, choose b∈B attaining d(a,B) and then c∈C attaining d(b,C). The triangle inequality gives d(a,C)≤d(a,B)+dH​(B,C). Taking the supremum over a, and doing the same with A,C exchanged, proves dH​(A,C)≤dH​(A,B)+dH​(B,C). Hence this is a metric.
The nested compact sets have the finite intersection property inside K1​, so K=⋂Kn​ is nonempty. It is a closed subset of K1​ and therefore compact. Because K⊆Kn​, only supx∈Kn​​d(x,K) contributes to the Hausdorff distance. If this did not tend to zero, some increasing indices nj​ and xj​∈Knj​​ would satisfy d(xj​,K)≥ϵ>0. A convergent subsequence in K1​ has limit x. For each fixed m, its tail belongs to the closed set Km​, so x∈K. But then d(xj​,K)≤∣xj​−x∣→0, a contradiction. Thus dH​(Kn​,K)→0​.

3G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 208 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 208
3G OurBigBook.com
Work over the finite field F2​. Reduce polynomials modulo Xi2​−Xi​, so their monomials are square-free. The binary Reed-Muller code RM(r,m) consists of the evaluation vectors of polynomials of degree at most r at all 2m points of F2m​, in a fixed order. This is a linear code of length 2m and dimension ∑j=0r​(jm​), for 0≤r≤m. Square-free monomials give independent evaluation functions, as follows inductively by splitting according to the last variable.
The minimum Hamming distance of a linear code equals its least nonzero Hamming weight. The result is
d(RM(r,m))=2m−r(0≤r≤m).​
(2)
Here r=0 is the repetition code, while r=m is the full binary vector space and has distance one. For the induction step, write f(x,t)=u(x)+tv(x), where degu≤r and degv≤r−1. Its evaluation vector is (u,u+v), the Reed-Muller bar-product recursion. If v=0, its nonzero Hamming weight is at least 2d(r,m−1)=2m−r, with the full-space endpoint treated as above. If v=0, every position where v=1 contributes exactly one to the sum of the two weights; hence the weight is at least wt(v)≥2(m−1)−(r−1)=2m−r. The monomial X1​⋯Xr​ is one exactly on 2m−r points, attaining the bound. Degrees greater than m give the same full code; the zero code at negative degree has no nonzero word whose weight could define a finite minimum.

This is a generalized linear model with independent Bernoulli distributions for the responses and the logit link. Under treatment coding with colour one as the reference level, the linear predictor is
log1−pi​pi​​=β0​+β2​1{ci​=2}​+β3​1{ci​=3}​+β4​1{ci​=4}​+βw​wi​.
(3)
Colour is a categorical variable, not a numerical trend. Width has the same slope for every colour, since no interaction term is fitted. The parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood estimation.
The approximate Wald confidence interval for the width coefficient is 0.46±1.96(0.106)​, or approximately (0.2522,0.6678). This uses the approximate normal distribution of the maximum-likelihood estimator, rather than a confidence interval for an individual binary response.
For the requested crab, the fitted linear predictor is η​=−11.38−0.22+0.46(20)=−2.40. Applying the inverse logit link gives p​=(1+e2.40)−1≃0.0832​. The rounded displayed coefficients need not reproduce the reported test statistics exactly.

i OurBigBook.com
Put x=1+y and retain linear terms. The delay differential equation is y˙​(t)=−αy(t−T), with characteristic equation of a delay differential equation λ+αe−λT=0. Write z=λT and q=αT. If a root has Rez≥0, then ∣z∣=qe−Rez≤q. Writing z=a+ib gives a=−qe−acosb. For q<π/2, ∣b∣<π/2 and the right side is negative, contradicting a≥0. All characteristic roots therefore lie in the left half-plane.
An imaginary root z=ib requires cosb=0 and b=qsinb. The first crossing is q=π/2, z=±iπ/2. Implicit differentiation gives dz/dq=−e−z/(1+z), whose real part at the positive crossing is (π/2)/(1+π2/4)>0. The later imaginary crossings occur at q=π/2+2πk and also enter the right half-plane. Thus the equilibrium is locally exponentially asymptotically stable when
αT<π/2,​
(4)
and unstable when αT>π/2. At equality the linearized equation has neutral oscillatory modes; it is the Hopf bifurcation threshold. If stability is meant for the nonlinear equation itself, the borderline can also be resolved. In dimensionless time s=t/T, let q0​=π/2. A small center oscillation has the form y=Rcosθ+R2(cos2θ/5+sin2θ/10)+O(R3). Substitution at quadratic order gives these second-harmonic coefficients. At cubic order the fundamental forcing is q0​R3(cosθ/20+3sinθ/20). Projection onto the center mode divides the complex forcing by the characteristic derivative 1+iq0​, yielding the Hopf normal form amplitude equation
dsdR​=−20(1+q02​)q0​(3q0​−1)​R3+O(R5).
(5)
Its cubic coefficient is negative, so the equilibrium at equality is locally asymptotically stable, with algebraic rather than exponential decay. Thus the usual strictly decaying linear condition is αT<π/2, while nonlinear local asymptotic stability includes αT=π/2. The purely imaginary linear modes alone would not justify that borderline conclusion.

ii

Words: 96 Articles: 1
5E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 96
ii OurBigBook.com
The delayed positive term models recruitment depending on the population a time T earlier; the quadratic negative term represents instantaneous density-dependent losses. Thus this delay differential equation delays recruitment rather than the strength of crowding acting on the present population.
With x=1+y, the linearized equation is y˙​=αy(t−T)−2αy(t). Its characteristic equation of a delay differential equation is λ+2α=αe−λT. A root with nonnegative real part would satisfy ∣λ+2α∣≥2α, whereas ∣αe−λT∣≤α. This is impossible. Consequently the equilibrium is locally exponentially asymptotically stable for every α>0 and T>0. There is no upper bound on αT in this model.

6B (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 228 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 228
6B OurBigBook.com
The Papperitz symbol describes a homogeneous second-order Fuchsian differential equation on the Riemann sphere, with three regular singular points and the two indicial exponents at each. At a finite point zj​, an exponent r corresponds locally to a factor (z−zj​)r; at infinity it corresponds to z−r. Repeated or resonant exponents can require logarithms. The six exponents obey the Fuchs relation that their sum is one. With three singularities there is no independent accessory parameter, so these data determine the normalized equation.
A Möbius transformation of a Papperitz symbol moves the singular points without changing their exponents. Multiplication of the dependent variable by a local power shifts the two exponents by that power, using the reciprocal local coordinate at infinity.
Set w=z/(z−1) and v(w)=F(a,c−b,c;w). At w=0,1,∞, the exponent pairs for v are respectively (0,1−c), (0,b−a), and (a,c−b). The Möbius transformation sends z=0,1,∞ to w=0,∞,1. Before rescaling, v(w(z)) therefore has exponent pairs (0,1−c) at zero, (a,c−b) at one, and (0,b−a) at infinity. Multiplication by (1−z)−a subtracts a at one and adds a at infinity. The resulting pairs are
(0,1−c),(0,c−a−b),(a,b),
(6)
exactly those of the original Gauss hypergeometric equation. Near zero choose the branch with (1−z)−a=1 at zero. The resulting solution is analytic there and has value one. Uniqueness of the normalized analytic solution yields
F(a,b,c;z)=(1−z)−aF(a,c−b,c;z/(z−1)).​
(7)
This is the Pfaff transformation. The normalization presupposes the usual admissible parameters, in particular c∈/{0,−1,−2,…}. Elsewhere the identity holds by analytic continuation with compatible branches, or by parameter limits wherever those are defined.

L=21​m(x˙12​+2x˙22​+x˙32​)−21​k[(x2​−x1​)2+(x3​−x2​)2].
(8)

mx¨1​=k(x2​−x1​),2mx¨2​=k(x1​−2x2​+x3​),mx¨3​=k(x2​−x3​).​

For a normal mode write xj​=Aj​eiωt. The generalized eigenvalue problem is
k​1−10​−12−1​0−11​​A=ω2mdiag(1,2,1)A.
(10)
The three independent eigenvectors and corresponding squared frequencies are
(1,1,1):0;(1,0,−1):k/m;(1,−1,1):2k/m.​
(11)
The last two have zero mass-weighted displacement and are orthogonal in the mass inner product. The lowest frequency is zero: it represents a rigid translation with both springs unchanged. Its general motion includes uniform centre-of-mass velocity, not just a constant displacement. Superpositions of the two oscillatory normal modes and this translation give the general solution.

8C (Cosmology)

Words: 284 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 284
8C OurBigBook.com
The effective number of relativistic energy degrees of freedom count two photon polarizations, four electron/positron spin states, and six neutrino/antineutrino states, with the Fermi-Dirac distribution factor 7/8 for fermions. Treating these species as relativistic and at a common temperature gives g∗​=2+(7/8)(4+6)=10.75​.
The mass-equivalent radiation mass density is ρ=(π2/30)g∗​(kB​T)4/(ℏ3c5). Therefore the Friedmann equation gives
H(T)=(45ℏ3c54π3Gg∗​​)1/2(kB​T)2.
(12)
At T0​=1010K, H0​≃0.503s−1. Equating the specified weak interaction rate to H0​(T/T0​)2 gives (T∗​/T0​)3=H0​/(1s−1) and hence
T∗​≃7.96×109K,T∗​∝g∗1/6​.​
(13)
The approximate equilibrium neutron-to-proton ratio, neglecting chemical potentials, is r∗​≃exp[−(mn​−mp​)c2/(kB​T∗​)], about 0.152 using the mass difference 1.293MeV. This is a freeze-out estimate rather than a detailed reaction-network computation.
After weak cosmological weak freeze-out, free neutrons undergo beta-minus decay; neutrinos decouple, and electron-positron annihilation heats the photons relative to the neutrinos. Initially the abundant energetic photons destroy deuterium almost as soon as it forms. Once the deuterium bottleneck ends, nuclear reactions rapidly pass through deuterium, tritium and helium-three to helium-4. Reactions eventually become too slow compared with cosmic expansion; nearly all surviving neutrons are bound in helium-four. Its mass fraction is approximately Y4​=2r/(1+r), where r is evaluated when nuclear assembly begins.
Increasing g∗​ increases the Hubble parameter, raises T∗​, increases the freeze-out neutron-to-proton ratio, and leaves less time for free-neutron decay after freeze-out. Both effects increase Y4​; decreasing g∗​ reverses them. Most deuterium is only an intermediate product and is burned into helium, so its residual abundance and its absolute change are tiny compared with the helium mass fraction. This does not imply a negligible fractional change in residual deuterium. Faster expansion also shortens the time available to burn it, and its relative abundance can be appreciably sensitive to extra radiation. The distinction matters when interpreting the final wording of the question; joint deuterium and helium abundances constrain extra relativistic species, as discussed in the Particle Data Group nucleosynthesis review.

The Chinese remainder theorem says that for pairwise coprime positive moduli ni​, arbitrary residue classes modulo each ni​ specify one residue class modulo ∏i​ni​. For an odd positive integer N=∏piei​​, the Jacobi symbol is (a/N)=∏i​(a/pi​)ei​, where each factor is a Legendre symbol; for N=1 the empty product is one. The Jacobi symbol is multiplicative in a, and is zero exactly when a and N have a common prime factor.

i OurBigBook.com
False. The Jacobi symbol (2/15)=(2/3)(2/5)=(−1)(−1)=1, yet 2 is not a quadratic residue modulo three. A solution modulo fifteen would give one modulo three, which is impossible. A positive Jacobi symbol need not indicate a square modulo a composite modulus.

ii OurBigBook.com
True. Since N is not a square, some exponent ei​ is odd. Choose a quadratic nonresidue modulo that pi​ and choose residue one at every other prime. The Chinese remainder theorem produces a unit b modulo N with (b/N)=−1. Multiplication by b permutes the residue classes modulo N. Thus, by multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol,
∑a=1N​(a/N)=∑a=1N​(ba/N)=−∑a=1N​(a/N).
(14)
The sum is therefore 0​. Nonunits contribute zero, so the permutation argument covers every term.

iii OurBigBook.com
False. The Carmichael number 561=3⋅11⋅17 supplies a counterexample. For every a coprime to 561, the Fermat little theorem gives a560≡1 modulo each of these primes, since 2,10,16 all divide 560. The Chinese remainder theorem then gives a560≡1(mod561). Thus the proposed Fermat primality test can fail to detect a composite for every coprime base.

iv

Words: 125 Articles: 1
9H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 125
iv OurBigBook.com
True. First suppose pe∣N with e≥2 maximal. By the Chinese remainder theorem, choose a≡1+pe−1(modpe) and a≡1 modulo all other prime-power factors. This is a unit, with Jacobi symbol one, because it is one modulo every prime. For m=(N−1)/2, the binomial theorem gives
am≡1+mpe−1≡1(modpe),
(15)
because p∤m and all higher terms contain pe. It is therefore a witness to the desired failure.
If N is square-free and composite, it has at least two prime factors. Choose a to be a quadratic nonresidue at one prime p and one at every other prime, again using the Chinese remainder theorem. Then (a/N)=−1. At a different odd prime q∣N, however, am≡1≡−1(modq). These two cases prove that every odd composite has an Euler-Jacobi witness, unlike the situation for the ordinary Fermat primality test.

Write Rj​=I−P−j​. Minimizing the residual sum of squares first over the coefficients of X−j​ reduces the problem to minimizing ∥Rj​Y−bRj​Xj​∥2. Full column rank ensures Rj​Xj​=0. Thus the partial regression formula and its variance are
β​j​=XjT​Rj​Xj​XjT​Rj​Y​,var(β​j​)=XjT​Rj​Xj​σ2​.​
(16)
This uses RjT​=Rj​=Rj2​ and the isotropic error covariance matrix σ2I.
Since the span of Xk​ is contained in the column space of X−j​, orthogonal projection onto the latter removes at least as much squared norm. Consequently
XjT​Rj​Xj​≤∥Xj​∥2−∥Xk​∥2(XkT​Xj​)2​,
(17)
and inversion proves the requested lower bound. Full rank makes the denominator positive.
Adding c1n​ to column j≥2 leaves the column space unchanged. Every old fitted vector is reproduced by keeping all slopes unchanged and replacing the regression intercept by β​1​−cβ​j​. Uniqueness of the ordinary least squares estimators then proves that slope j is unchanged. In particular all columns can be centered by such changes. Applying the previous projection argument to the centered design proves the bound with Xj​−Xˉj​1n​ and Xk​−Xˉk​1n​; the normalized inner product is now the usual sample correlation.
Each reported coefficient test is the two-sided Student's t-test of H0​:βj​=0 against H1​:βj​=0, conditional on the other predictors. Under the null, β​j​/(σ(XTX)jj−1​​) has a Student's t-distribution with 100−3=97 degrees of freedom. At five percent the intercept is significant, but neither individual test slope is. The final F-test compares the full model against an intercept-only model: H0​:βMaths​=βStats​=0. It has (2,97) degrees of freedom and rejects at five percent, since its p-value is 0.003166. Thus the predictors jointly explain variation, without strong evidence separating their individual conditional effects.
The two test predictors have sample correlation 0.9371630, although each has only moderate correlation with the final exam response. The variance inflation factor is 1/(1−0.93716302)≃8.22. Their nearly shared direction produces substantial multicollinearity, inflating the individual slope standard errors. The joint F-test can detect this common predictive direction even though either coefficient, given the other, has a large p-value.

dtd​Ef(x)=E[Ai​∂i​f+21​Bij​∂i​∂j​f].

We use the decay and absence of boundary flux intended in the question, sufficiently strong to remove the moment-weighted boundary terms. For f=xk​, only ∂i​f=δik​ survives, giving d⟨xk​⟩/dt=⟨Ak​⟩. The three jump vectors and their rates are (1,0) at rate λ, (−1,1) at rate γx1​, and (0,−1) at rate βx2​. Summing rate times jump gives the Fokker-Planck drift vector, while summing rate times the outer product of the jump gives the Fokker-Planck diffusion matrix:
A=(λ−γx1​γx1​−βx2​​),B=(λ+γx1​−γx1​​−γx1​γx1​+βx2​​).​

The maturation event simultaneously decreases larvae and increases adults; this accounts for the negative off-diagonal entries. Since A is affine, its expectation is its value at the mean. Setting both mean derivatives to zero yields ⟨x1​⟩=λ/γ,⟨x2​⟩=λ/β​.

13I (Logic and Set Theory)

The Axiom of foundation states that every nonempty set A has a member a with a∩A=∅. The principle of epsilon induction states that a formula ϕ satisfying ∀x[(∀y∈xϕ(y))⇒ϕ(x)] holds for every set x.
Assume Axiom of foundation and suppose a progressive formula has a counterexample a. In the transitive closure of {a}, use axiom schema of separation to collect the counterexamples into a nonempty set B. Foundation supplies b∈B having no member in B. Since the closure is transitive, every member of b satisfies ϕ, contradicting progressiveness. Conversely, if a nonempty set A had no foundation-minimal member, every x∈A would have a member y∈x∩A. The formula x∈/A is then progressive: if every member of x lies outside A, x cannot belong to A. Epsilon induction would make A empty, a contradiction. This proves equivalence in the presence of the other Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory.
To obtain the cumulative hierarchy, perform epsilon induction on the assertion that x belongs to some Vα​. If this holds for each member y, Axiom schema of replacement collects their least such ordinals into a set. Choose an ordinal β above them all. Then x⊆Vβ​ and x∈Vβ+1​. Thus every set occurs in the hierarchy. Use the rank of a set convention rk(x)=supy∈x​(rk(y)+1), equivalently the least α with x⊆Vα​.

14I OurBigBook.com
A matching in a graph from X to Y is a collection of edges with disjoint endpoints covering every vertex of X; equivalently it chooses a distinct neighbour in Y for each x∈X. For a finite bipartite graph, the Hall marriage theorem says this exists exactly when ∣N(A)∣≥∣A∣ for every A⊆X. Necessity follows by counting the distinct matched neighbours.
For sufficiency, induct on ∣X∣. If a nonempty proper subset A is tight, ∣N(A)∣=∣A∣, Hall's condition holds on (A,N(A)). It also holds on (X∖A,Y∖N(A)): for B⊆X∖A, the original condition applied to A∪B gives ∣N(B)∖N(A)∣≥∣B∣. Induction provides two disjoint matching in a graph whose union covers X. If no nonempty proper subset is tight, choose an edge xy, possible by Hall's condition. Delete its endpoints. Each nonempty subset of X∖{x} had at least one extra neighbour, so deleting y leaves Hall's condition intact. Induction and then the edge xy finish the proof. The single-vertex case is immediate.
For the degree condition, fix A⊆X and double-count with weights:
∣N(A)∣≥∑y∈N(A)​d(y)dA​(y)​=∑x∈A​∑y∼x​d(y)1​≥∑x∈A​d(x)d(x)​=∣A∣.
(32)
Every denominator is nonzero; the last inequality uses d(y)≤d(x) along each edge. The Hall marriage theorem therefore proves the required matching exists. Finiteness, as in the usual course version of the theorem, is understood; the same proof covers a finite X with arbitrary Y and finite degrees.

A one-dimensional continuous group representation is a continuous group homomorphism ρ:S1→C×. Its image is compact. If some ∣ρ(z)∣ differed from one, its positive or negative powers would be unbounded, so the image lies in S1. Lift t↦ρ(eit) to a continuous real argument a(t) with a(0)=0. Then a(s+t)−a(s)−a(t) is a continuous integer multiple of 2π and vanishes at (0,0), hence is always zero. The continuous Cauchy functional equation gives a(t)=ct. Periodicity forces e2πic=1, so c=n∈Z. Consequently ρ(z)=zn​; conversely every such map is a continuous one-dimensional group representation.

OK×​≅μ(K)×Zr1​+r2​−1,

where μ(K) is the finite group of roots of unity in K. Thus an imaginary quadratic number field has only roots of unity as units: usually {±1}, with four for d=−1 and six for d=−3. A real quadratic number field has units ±ϵn for a fundamental unit ϵ>1 and integers n.
For K=Q(26​), OK​=Z[26​] and the field norm is x2−26y2. The element ϵ=5+26​ has norm −1 and is a unit. It is the smallest positive unit greater than one. Indeed for 1<u<ϵ, its conjugate is ±1/u, so the coefficient y=(u∓1/u)/(226​) is a positive integer less than two. Therefore y=1, and x2=26±1 forces x=5, giving u=ϵ, a contradiction. The Dirichlet unit theorem now gives OK×​={±(5+26​)n:n∈Z}​. Its least positive norm-one generator is ϵ2=51+1026​.
For the generalized Pell equation, write α=x+y26​ with norm N=±10. Change the sign if necessary and multiply by a power of ϵ to place it in 10​≤α<ϵ10​. These operations preserve integrality and the absolute norm, though the latter operation can change the norm's sign. Since α′=N/α, we have x=(α+N/α)/2≥0 and y=(α−N/α)/(226​)≥0. The upper bound gives y<4. Checking y=0,1,2,3 in x2=26y2±10 leaves only (x,y)=(4,1),(6,1). Both reduced elements lie in the chosen interval. Therefore all integral solutions of either sign are
x+y26​=±(4+26​)(5+26​)nor±(6+26​)(5+26​)n,n∈Z.​
(36)
Negative powers are integral because ϵ−1=26​−5. In the first family the norm is −10(−1)n and in the second it is 10(−1)n, so this also separates the two equations. The reduction proves exhaustion rather than merely generating examples.

Here one must distinguish two conventions for a radical extension. The solvability theorem says that a finite extension with solvable normal-closure Galois group is contained in a tower of radical adjunctions. Under the convention that this containment defines a radical extension, this is the requested assertion.
Let N/K be the finite normal closure and let m be divisible by the orders of its Galois group elements. Adjoin a primitive mth root of unity, obtaining K′=K(ζm​), which itself is a radical adjunction since ζmm​=1. The Galois group of NK′/K′ embeds in the solvable group of N/K, so it is solvable. A composition series with cyclic prime-order quotients gives a tower of cyclic prime-degree extensions above K′. Each is a radical adjunction, as the following argument shows.
For a cyclic extension E/F of prime degree p containing ζp​, let σ generate its Galois group. The F-linear operator σ satisfies Xp−1, a product of distinct linear factors in characteristic zero. Thus it is diagonalizable. Because σ=1, it has an eigenvector a=0 with eigenvalue ζpj​=1. Then ap∈F and a∈/F, so E=F(a) by primeness of the degree. Applying this at every step produces a radical tower containing L.
If “radical extension” instead means that L/K itself must be such a tower, the printed statement is false without this qualification. For example the real cubic subfield of Q(ζ7​) is cyclic and solvable, but contains no nonrational a with an∈Q: all three conjugates are real roots of the same equation Xn=an, which has at most two real roots, while any nonrational element of the cubic field has three distinct conjugates. Consequently no nontrivial radical adjunction can start a tower inside it. Containment in a radical tower is the valid general conclusion.

The Artin–Schreier polynomial is irreducible: if r∈K solved it, a finite pole of r would create a pole of even order in r2+r, impossible for t; at infinity a pole of r likewise gives even order, while t has order one. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence for K=M∪N is the long exact sequence in homology
⋯→Hn​(M∩N)(i∗​,−j∗​)​Hn​(M)⊕Hn​(N)k∗​+l∗​​Hn​(K)∂n​​Hn−1​(M∩N)→⋯.

We use integer coefficients. A simplicial cycle c in K can be written c=m+n with chains in M,N. Since ∂m=−∂n, this chain lies in M∩N and is a cycle. Define ∂n​[c]=[∂m]; changing the splitting or the cycle representative changes this by a boundary, giving a well-defined connecting homomorphism.
First consider two acyclic subcomplexes. Their intersection is either empty or acyclic. If empty, positive-degree homology of their disjoint union vanishes. If nonempty, the reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence implies the same conclusion, including degree one since the intersection has zero reduced H0​. This proves the claim for two subcomplexes.
Inductively let U=M1​∪⋯∪Mn−1​, V=Mn​, and W=U∩V=⋃i<n​(Mi​∩Mn​). Discard empty members as necessary. Both U and W satisfy the same intersection hypothesis with at most n−1 members, so their homology vanishes in degrees at least n−2. The exact segment Hi​(U)⊕Hi​(V)→Hi​(K)→Hi−1​(W) then gives Hi​(K)=0 for i≥n−1​. For n≥3 these degrees are positive and the induction applies directly; empty W again means a disjoint union.
For sharpness, take the boundary of an (n−1)-simplex, covered by its n facets. Every nonempty proper intersection of facets is a simplex and thus has the homology of a point; the intersection of all facets is empty. The union is a sphere Sn−2 and Hn−2​ is nonzero. For n=2 it is two isolated vertices and H0​≅Z2; for n≥3, Hn−2​≅Z. The degree bound cannot be lowered.

i OurBigBook.com
For a smooth projective algebraic curve, a linear system of divisors comes from a finite-dimensional space V⊆H0(C,O(D)). A basis of sections s0​,…,sn​ defines f(P)=[s0​(P):⋯:sn​(P)], using any local trivialization; a common scalar change does not alter the projective point. A base-point-free linear system makes this defined everywhere, and f∗OPn​(1)≅O(D). Pulling back a hyperplane gives the zero divisor of a linear combination of the sections, an element of the original system.
A system with base divisor B can instead define a map after removing B, but its hyperplane pullbacks have class D−B. Thus base-point-freeness is needed for the stated original-system property. For a closed immersion, the system must also separate distinct points and tangent directions; equivalently it is a very ample linear system. On a smooth curve the latter tangent condition is separation of the length-two subscheme at each point.

Weak convergence Xk​⇒X means that Ef(Xk​)→Ef(X) for every bounded continuous real function f on Rd; it is a statement about their distributions, not their coupling.
The central limit theorem says that for independent identically distributed real variables of finite mean μ and variance σ2, n​(Xˉn​−μ)⇒N(0,σ2). For σ>0 this is equivalent to convergence of (∑Xj​−nμ)/(σn​) to the standard normal distribution. For σ=0, every variable equals μ almost surely and the limit is the point mass at zero.
For the proof when σ>0, put Y=(X−μ)/σ. Its characteristic function has expansion φY​(t)=1−t2/2+o(t2). To justify this using only a second moment, subtract the first two Taylor terms of eitY and use dominated convergence theorem, with the second-order remainder bounded by a constant times t2Y2. Independence gives the characteristic function of the normalized sum as [φY​(t/n​)]n→e−t2/2. The Lévy continuity theorem says that pointwise convergence of characteristic functions to a characteristic function continuous at zero implies weak convergence. Since e−t2/2 is the characteristic function of N(0,1), the result follows.

The nonparametric bootstrap sample is a sample of size n drawn independently with replacement from the empirical distribution Fn​=n−1∑i​δXi​​, conditional on the observed data. To simulate it, take independent uniform Uj​ and set Xjb​=X1+⌊nUj​⌋​, assigning Uj​=1 to the last index if it occurs in a finite-precision generator.
Let Gnb​ be the conditional cumulative distribution function of n​(Xˉnb​−Xˉn​), and let qn​(p)=inf{t:Gnb​(t)≥p}. A basic bootstrap confidence interval is
Cn​=[Xˉn​−qn​(1−α/2)/n​, Xˉn​−qn​(α/2)/n​].​
(50)
In practice the conditional quantiles are estimated from many simulated bootstrap means; the asymptotic argument below describes exact bootstrap quantiles or a simulation count tending to infinity.
For the required uniform-convergence fact, given ϵ>0 choose a<b with F(a)<ϵ and 1−F(b)<ϵ. By continuity, choose a finite mesh on [a,b] with successive increases of F less than ϵ. Pointwise convergence at the mesh points makes ∣Fn​−F∣<ϵ there for large n. Monotonicity sandwiches both functions between their neighbouring mesh values, so ∣Fn​(t)−F(t)∣<2ϵ throughout [a,b]. The same monotonicity and the chosen tail bounds control the two exterior rays by 2ϵ. Hence supt​∣Fn​(t)−F(t)∣→0.
The bootstrap consistency theorem for the sample mean states that, for iid observations with 0<σ2<∞, the conditional law of n​(Xˉnb​−Xˉn​) converges weakly, in probability, to N(0,σ2). By continuity of that limiting distribution and the preceding monotonicity argument, the convergence of conditional distribution functions is uniform in probability. Since the limit is strictly increasing, qn​(p)→σΦ−1(p) in probability for 0<p<1. The coverage event is
qn​(α/2)≤n​(Xˉn​−μ)≤qn​(1−α/2).
(51)
The central limit theorem, quantile convergence and Slutsky theorem therefore give PN(μ∈Cn​)→1−α​.
Positive variance is needed for this exact coverage conclusion. If the finite variance allowed in the wording is zero, all observations equal μ almost surely and the interval collapses to {μ}, with coverage one. The bootstrap distribution is still consistent with the degenerate limit, but a nonrandomized usual interval cannot then have limiting coverage 1−α for 0<α<1.

A horseshoe for an interval map consists of two branches covering a common interval: there are an open interval J and disjoint open subintervals K0​,K1​⊆J with f(K0​)=f(K1​)=J. Equivalently one can work with two closed intervals with disjoint interiors whose images cover their union, and then restrict the branches. Glendinning chaos means that some positive iterate fm has such a horseshoe, rather than requiring one for f itself.
For the three-cycle, use the intermediate value theorem on endpoint images. The interval covering relations are Ia​→Ib​ and Ib​→Ia​,Ib​. Consequently both f2(Ia​) and f2(Ib​) cover Ia​∪Ib​. This proves f2 has a horseshoe. The directed covering graph of an interval map has exactly these forced arrows; a closed walk a→b→b→a has length three and a primitive itinerary. Pulling back the intervals successively and using the fixed-point property produces a point fixed by f3 with this itinerary. It cannot be fixed by f, and a shared endpoint belongs to the already given three-cycle, so a genuine period-three orbit results.
For the increasing spatial order of the five-cycle, let Ij​=[xj−1​,xj​], 1≤j≤4. The forced graph is
I1​→I2​→I3​→I4​,I4​→I1​,I2​,I3​,I4​.
(63)
The primitive loops I4​, I3​I4​, I2​I3​I4​, and I1​I2​I3​I4​ force exact periods 1,2,3,4​. For periods below five the known five-cycle endpoints cannot be responsible, so the interval itineraries give distinct interior orbits. Both g2(I3​) and g2(I4​) cover I3​∪I4​, so g is guaranteed to be Glendinning-chaotic.
A horseshoe for g itself is not guaranteed. As a counterexample put xj​=j on [0,4] and interpolate by g(x)=x+1 for 0≤x≤3, g(x)=16−4x for 3≤x≤4. This has the required five-cycle. The unique fixed point is 16/5, with g(x)>x to its left and g(x)<x to its right. Any nondegenerate closed interval whose image covers itself must contain this fixed point in its interior: an interval entirely on either side, or with the fixed point as an endpoint, fails to cover its extreme endpoint. Two intervals with disjoint interiors therefore cannot both cover themselves, as a horseshoe would require. Hence this example has no one-iterate horseshoe.
For the alternative spatial order, set y0​=x4​,y1​=x2​,y2​=x1​,y3​=x3​,y4​=x0​ and Jj​=[yj−1​,yj​]. Endpoint images give
J1​→J4​,J2​→J2​,J3​,J3​→J1​,J4​→J1​,J2​.
(64)
The self-loop at J2​, the two-cycle J1​J4​, and the four-cycle J2​J3​J1​J4​ force 1,2,4​; period three is not guaranteed. To see this last claim, take the connect-the-dots map at yj​=j with values (4,3,1,0,2). Its exact interval transitions are those displayed. Any length-three closed itinerary is the repeated self-loop in J2​; there the map is the affine decreasing function 5−2x, whose third iterate has only its original fixed point. Endpoints belong to the five-cycle. Thus no exact three-cycle exists in this example.
Chaos is still guaranteed: from J2​ there are two different length-four closed walks, four self-loops and J2​J3​J1​J4​J2​. Pullbacks give disjoint branches of g4 over a common interval in J2​, hence a horseshoe for an interval map for an iterate. A horseshoe for g itself is again not guaranteed: the same connect-the-dots example is strictly decreasing on [0,3] and increasing on [3,4] with image [0,2]. Its unique fixed point is 5/3, again with g(x)>x to the left and g(x)<x to the right. The same fixed-point argument rules out two self-covering intervals with disjoint interiors. These counterexamples distinguish the three separate questions about periods, chaos and a one-iterate horseshoe.

Radial null curves obey −fdu2−2dudr=0. For their unparameterized paths,
drdu​=0ordrdu​=−f2​.​
(83)
Inside the horizon, the first family satisfies dt/dr=1/f, so dr/dt=f>0 and is outgoing. The second satisfies dt/dr=−1/f and is ingoing. Integrating gives u=u0​ for outgoing rays and u=C−2aartanh(r/a) for ingoing rays. The null paths are geodesics after suitable reparameterization; for example in the two-dimensional radial metric each null direction has covariant acceleration proportional to itself.
To show constant-u rays at the requested angle, the diagram uses vertical plotting coordinate u+r and horizontal r, with equal scale. This is the stated tilted u grid: constant u becomes a line of slope one. The ingoing curves bend to decreasing u+r as r approaches the horizon.

For a radial timelike geodesic, the static Killing energy is E=ft˙ and normalization gives r˙2=E2−f. Choose E=2​ and start at r(0)=0 with outward velocity one. An explicit trajectory is
r(τ)=asinh(τ/a).​
(84)
It solves r˙2=1+r2/a2 and reaches r=a at τH​=aarsinh(1)<∞​. Differentiating the energy equation gives r¨=r/a2, the radial geodesic equation, so this is an actual freely falling trajectory.
The regular coordinate satisfies u˙=(E−r˙)/f=1/(E+r˙), which is finite and positive at the crossing. Together with u(τ)=u(0)+∫0τ​[2​+cosh(s/a)]−1ds, the trajectory extends through the horizon in the regular chart. Divergence of the static time there does not imply infinite proper time.

To recover the printed dispersion relation, interpret the surface maintained flat as an imposed flat upper boundary for the perturbation, so its normal velocity is zero. This is the rigid-lid approximation. Work with perturbation velocity potentials ϕ−​=Aekyeikx+σt below the interface and ϕ+​=Bcosh[k(y−h)]eikx+σt in the upper layer. They solve the Laplace equation, decay as y→−∞, and obey ∂y​ϕ+​(h)=0.
The linear kinematic boundary conditions at the interface give (σ+ikU)η0​=kA and ση0​=−kBsinh(kh). Equality of pressures, using the linear Bernoulli equation, gives (σ+ikU)A=σBcosh(kh). The equal fluid densities cancel the interface gravitational restoring term. Eliminating A,B,η0​ yields
(σ+ikU)2+σ2coth(kh)=0.​
(85)
With q=tanh(kh), the roots are
σ=1+qUk​(−iq±q​),Reσ=±1+tanh(kh)Uktanh(kh)​​.​
(86)
For every k>0 one root has positive real part. Thus the vortex sheet has a Kelvin-Helmholtz instability at every wavelength in this model. If kh≫1, q→1 and the growing rate is Uk/2. If kh≪1, q∼kh and it is Ukkh​.
There is a physical qualification to the wording. A dynamically deformable free surface at finite gravity is not exactly a flat lid. Its linear conditions combine to σ2ϕ+​(h)+g∂y​ϕ+​(h)=0. Writing the upper potential as Bcosh(ky)+Csinh(ky) and using the same interface conditions instead gives
(σ+ikU)2[σ2+gktanh(kh)]+σ2[σ2tanh(kh)+gk]=0.
(87)
The stated quadratic follows in the strong-gravity flat-surface limit, or with the flat condition imposed exactly. It is not the exact dispersion relation of a freely moving upper surface at arbitrary finite g. This makes explicit the boundary interpretation needed for the requested formula.

Linearizing the shallow water equations about depth h at rest gives wave speed c=gh​. Replacing h by c in the nonlinear equations yields ct​+ucx​+(c/2)ux​=0 and ut​+uux​+2ccx​=0. Direct addition and subtraction give
[∂t​+(u±c)∂x​][u±2(c−c0​)]=0.
(88)
Thus the Riemann invariants J±​=u±2(c−c0​) are constant on the characteristics C±​ with speeds u±c. In this problem c0​=gh0​​.

ii OurBigBook.com
The release produces a rarefaction wave expanding into the dry region. Every incoming C−​ characteristic connects to the undisturbed pool, where J−​=0, so throughout the simple wave u=2(c−c0​). The outgoing C+​ rays emanate from (0,0) and have x/t=u+c=3c−2c0​. Solving gives
c=31​(x/t+2c0​),u=32​(x/t−c0​),−2c0​t≤x≤c0​t.​
(89)
The depth is h=c2/g. At the right edge these formulas match the stationary pool; at the left edge c=0 and the fluid front travels at −2c0​. Beyond it the bed is dry, so a fluid velocity need not be assigned. Values at t=0 are understood as one-sided limits of the fan.
The first wall interaction occurs at t0​=a/c0​. The leftmost reflected signal follows a C−​ ray through (a,t0​). Until a point has encountered this signal it remains in the original fan. In that fan its speed is u−c=x/(3t)−4c0​/3. Thus
x˙−3tx​=−34c0​​,x(t)=Ct1/3−2c0​t.
(90)
Matching at (a,t0​) gives the reflected front
xf​(t)=3a(c0​t/a)1/3−2c0​t.​
(91)
Consequently the same rarefaction formula remains valid for −2c0​t≤x≤xf​(t) when t≥t0​. Between xf​(t) and the wall, information from the wall changes J−​ and the simple-wave relation no longer holds. In particular continuing the old formula to x=a would give a negative velocity for t>t0​, violating the no-penetration condition u(a,t)=0. The reflected region must accommodate both characteristic families; it is not another untouched part of the original fan.

The Krylov subspace is Km​(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Am−1v}. Let s be the first index for which Asv depends linearly on v,…,As−1v. Such an index exists with 1≤s≤n, since v=0 and any n+1 vectors are dependent. The first s vectors are independent. The relation for Asv shows that their span is invariant under A: multiplying any generator by A stays in that span. Repeated multiplication makes every higher power stay there too. Therefore
dimKm​=m (m≤s),dimKm​=s (m>s).​
(92)
Once a Krylov subspace stops growing, it cannot resume growth.

Let the distinct eigenvalues be λ1​,…,λs′​. Distinct-eigenvalue eigenvectors are independent. A relation ∑k=0m−1​ak​Akv=0 becomes ∑i​ci​p(λi​)wi​=0, with p(z)=∑k<m​ak​zk. Since every ci​=0, it requires p(λi​)=0 for every i. No nonzero polynomial of degree below s′ has that many distinct roots. Thus the first s′ powers are independent, while ∏i​(A−λi​I)v=0 gives the next dependence. Hence s=s′​. Equivalently the coefficients of these powers form a full-rank Vandermonde matrix through this index.

Solution

Words: 227
b OurBigBook.com
The linear-system residual at an approximate solution xm​ is rm​=b−Axm​. For symmetric positive definite A, the Conjugate gradient method has xm​∈x0​+Km​(A,r0​) and minimizes the squared A-norm of the error over that affine space; its residual is orthogonal to Km​(A,r0​).
If A has t distinct eigenvalues, interpolate q(λ)=1/λ on them with a polynomial of degree at most t−1. The finite-dimensional spectral theorem gives A−1=q(A), so the exact correction x∗​−x0​=A−1r0​ lies in Kt​(A,r0​). The minimum possible error at step t is therefore zero. Thus CG terminates in at most t steps​ in exact arithmetic, possibly earlier if the initial residual has fewer eigencomponents. If r0​=0, it terminates immediately.
A symmetric positive definite matrix preconditioner M changes the system to M−1/2AM−1/2z=M−1/2b, with x=M−1/2z; practical preconditioned CG applies solves with M. It can accelerate convergence by reducing the spectral condition number of a positive-definite matrix, which improves the usual bound involving (κ​−1)/(κ​+1), and by clustering eigenvalues, which allows low-degree residual polynomials small on the spectrum even when the extreme-eigenvalue bound is pessimistic.
Choosing M=A​ makes the transformed matrix I, so one step suffices. But applying M−1 already requires solving the original problem, and constructing an exact factorization generally incurs its original computational cost. It is therefore not a useful shortcut for a single unsolved system, though an available factorization can be reused for multiple right-hand sides. Effective matrix preconditioning balances spectral improvement against inexpensive application.
